title: Awareness of Diversity
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: As we deepen our connection with nature, our perception of the world shifts, allowing us to see its subtleties and complexity with greater clarity. This process involves cultivating awareness and recognition, rather than just accumulating knowledge, and it's made possible through a practice that allows us to approach life with an open and receptive attitude - like "still hunting" in meditation, where we let go of preconceptions and allow ourselves to be present with our surroundings. Through direct experience and observation, we can gain true understanding of the world around us, just as we might recognize a rare bird species through clear perception. This kind of insight is essential for living a more compassionate life, one that values connection and recognition over preconceived notions or intellectual knowledge.

sentences.text: Good evening.
This is one of those things where you are typing and you press print and then you run out the door to the zazen session.
I hope that it makes any kind of sense.
We'll find out.
Dogen said:
*Although there are many features in the dusty world and the world beyond conditions, you see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.
In order to learn the nature of the myriad things, you must know that although they may look round or square, the other features of oceans and mountains are infinite in variety.
Whole worlds are there.
It is so not only around you, but also directly beneath your feet or in a drop of water.*
This morning I looked out my window and I saw that this pair of mating mallards were back, who had been on my seasonal wetland last year.
Or at least I figured it was the same pair, because I know that animals are individuals like us and they have very particular habits.
There was a sense of recognition, a sense of "hi, welcome back."
But then they suddenly jumped up and flew away, and maybe they'll be back tomorrow morning.
It was a little bit like this last winter.
I went out birding with my friend Jim for the Audubon Christmas Bird Count.
We pulled off to the side of the road, because we have to do a lot of this from the car, just at something that looked like a likely spot.
We were glassing over the field and up jumps this hovering bird, hanging for a good moment right over us.
It was a Northern Shrike.
It's about a Robin-sized bird.
It's a mean little predator that will catch other birds on the wing and then impale them on a thorn or a spike of a branch, to sort of eviscerate them there.
But at the end of the day, like birders do, we tallied up what we'd done and we declared that the Shrike was our bird of the day.
It's really subjective, what birders call their bird of the day.
It can be a rare bird, or we saw a really rare bird, or some interesting moment when you saw it.
But it generally has something to do with this clear perception, like a bird that you've got a really good look at or that presented itself to you in an encountering sort of way.
And that was this bird for us that day.
The first day that I occupied my farm, more than a quarter century ago, I was standing in the front yard with the former owner.
He was showing me around and he said, "We get wood ducks here sometime.
In fact, there's one right there," and he pointed up in the top of this big yellow birch tree.
Well, I've never seen a wood duck on my farm since, but the imagination in my mind of that wood duck still lives for me there.
And I look at that tree, which is a decrepit tree.
Some people would cut it down because it keeps dropping branches and knocking the power line out.
But I want to keep it there because I think the duck's going to come back.
A long time ago, I used to tell myself that I had this aversion to science.
I was an arts guy, and I just didn't like the way, to my mind, science divided the world up and named every part.
It removed the romantic gloss of interconnectedness that I was imagining about the world.
But my poetry professor in Tucson really disabused me of this.
He took us out into the desert for an exercise.
Most of us kids were from northern states, and we weren't familiar with the environment around there.
He said, "I want you to sit down.
I want you to write a short description of what you're looking at."
A bush with sticks jutting out, messy, dusty, hot, bland colored, rocky.
Our descriptions lacked particularity.
We didn't know any of the names.

He walked us around then for about 15 minutes and gave us a little tour and described features, named a variety of plants, went into a little bit of geology, a little bit about desert morphology and whatnot.
Then he sat us down and had us do the descriptive exercise again.
And everything had gained this clear focus.
We now were able to write and actually see that, wait, this bush is separate from that other thing that's coming through it.
And maybe we were able to throw a name here and there.
But the striking thing was that the particularity of our understanding of the environment had suddenly heightened.
There were literally things there that we seemingly had not been able to see before.
I think about my eyesight: the Department of Motor Vehicles claims that it's not that good, and when I look in their little machine, that seems true.
But I know that I can tell the difference between a crow and a raven on the wing from literally about half a mile away.
So there are different orders of seeing, aren't there?
It's experience, it's knowledge, but mostly it's this deep intimacy with understanding differences.
Here's a story I like to remember from a long time ago.
My ex-partner, Jackie, used to work for the Lummi Tribe in education.
She had to travel back and forth a lot from the res up to Ferndale, where a lot of the Lummi kids were going to school in the public schools there.
So she'd drive back and forth across Lummi flats.
One day she was doing that with a coworker who was a Lummi woman and had lived there her whole life.
Jackie said, "Oh, there's a red-tailed hawk."
And the woman said, "I always called that a bald eagle."
A little ways down the road Jackie said, "Oh, there's a great blue heron."
And the woman said, "I always called that a raven."
Then, a little ways down the road, Jackie said, "There's a marsh hawk."
And the woman said, "I always called that a robin."
It turned out, with a little more talk and a little more inquiry, that Jackie found out this woman only knew the names of three birds: bald eagle, raven, and robin.
And whatever bird she saw, it was going to be one of those three.
We like to praise our kids, so I'm just going to brag about my kid a little bit.
When he was little, really little, before he could talk, he learned half the birds in the North American field.
How do I know that?
At that time he was reading board books, the kind of books where you open them up and he points at it and you go, "That's a cow."
He points at it and you go, "That's a bird."
Then when they get a little better at it, you say, "Show me the bird," and they point at it.
One day he half crawled, tottled, scooted over and grabbed the bird field guide off this low table and brought it over and plopped down in my lap.
He knows that I look at this book a lot, and what he's saying is, "Let's read this book."
So you can't just say "bird, bird, bird, bird," right?
You've got to get a little more particular.
So I'm saying, "Well, that's a least bittern.
That's a spotted sandpiper.
That's a [unclear: "fair genus hawk"]."
I'd come home from work every day and go see him, and usually I'd grab him and head outside for a minute and do a little connect time.
One day I had him walking around outside, and we had this barred owl who would hoot a lot from the far side of the meadow in the evening.
That was something I used to hang out with him and listen to.
But I'm talking to him this day and I say, "This morning when I got up I heard a great horned owl from over here, not the barred owl from over there."
And he takes his hands and puts them on top of his head, and he points in the direction I was pointing with the great horned owl.
And I go, "Yeah, the great horned owl, sure, that's what you're talking about."
So we go inside, we take the book, open up the book.
There's half a dozen owls on that page and he points at the great horned owl.
He puts his hands on his head like that.
It turned out that he had started to learn the birds so well that I could ask him half the birds in the book and he would get them right before he could talk.

Later, as he got older, like five, he actually forgot all of that knowledge, which was quite a lesson in the elasticity of the human mind, that you would learn something so well at age two and forget it by age five.
But he was devoting his time to the different types of heavy equipment and orders of dinosaurs and things like that.
But when he could talk, I remember taking him outside again another day.
Maybe little kids can see like hawks or something, but I remember having him in my arms and his head fell back and he looked up in the sky and he said, "Bulk eagle!"
And it was so far up there you would never have noticed it, but it was way up there.
And he saw it.
Or this one time I went out to his sandbox, where you just hang out and he'd be playing with the trucks in the sand.
There was a suet ball hanging from the apple tree there, and the willow swamp is just about 20 yards away.
There's this bird that calls out at the swamp, goes, "Charlie!"
And he's just playing and he goes, "Oh, that's a little purple bird."
I said, "You mean a purple finch?"
He goes, "Yeah, it's a little purple bird.
That's Forrest's favorite bird."
And I'm like, huh, I had no idea.
So I go inside and I get the book and there's a description and it says, "makes a musical churly sound."
I didn't know that it was called that.
He had taken his observational skills into a completely improvisational phase.

He had literally probably seen the bird come to the suet ball, watched it fly away, noticed the song and just learned all that on his own, because from this exercise with the bird book and all this learning, he had this sense that there's a lot of things to know in the world.
There's a great many things to know.
There's probably things I don't know, and there's more to learn all the time.
So what does this have to do with practice?
Well, everything really.
It's important to know.
It's not so important to know all the names of everything, but it's important to know that there are many things we don't know.
It's awareness of diversity.
It's a key to our practice.
There's a variety of emotions and thoughts that are never ending.
Without a sensitivity to the diversity that's inside of us, we tend to circle back into loops and habits that are limited and narrow, as if we only knew Robin or Raven or Eagle.
You see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.
So awareness of diversity comes to us through various levels of sight.
There's peripheral vision, what we catch out of the corner of our eye, so to speak.
There's encountering vision, where something looks our way and we look at it and our eyes connect and there's some sense of recognition.
There are tricks of the ear and the eye, like how far off a rustling sound is, but it suddenly becomes our own breath or our heartbeat.
There's apparitional vision, something that appears as if it's there but not there, and it's gone.
Was it even there?
Once I was standing in a meadow at really deep dusk and I saw a heron, but a half-sized heron, come flying in low to roost in the swamp, and it was gone in the dark.
I thought, did I see it?
Did I not see it?
I still see it now.
I saw it that one time, and I still see it.
I want to make it into a black-crowned night heron, but the range map tells me no, maybe an American bittern.
I have a quote here.
This is a wonderful book of interviews with Gary Snyder.
It's called The Real Work.
Snyder is really quite amazing in conversation.
The interviewer is asking whether you get inspiration for poems, or whether poems get generated in meditation.

*The question is, there's a book around called Zen and the Art of Archery by Eugene [unclear: "Harigol"], which says that through a kind of disciplined inattention, the archer and the target become one.
The artist and the creation become one.
Do you find that meditation has worked this way for you?*
Snyder says:
*Well, yes, because like I say, I never try to use meditation deliberately for the reason that, as anyone who has done much meditation knows, what you aim at is never what you hit.
What you consciously aim at is never what you get.
Your conscious mind can't do it for you.
So you do have to practice a kind of detached and careful but really relaxed inattention, which lets the unconscious do its own thing of rising and manifesting itself.
But the moment you reach out, it's like peripheral vision almost.
The moment you reach out to grab it, it slips back.
It's like hunting.
It's like still hunting.
Still hunting is when you take a stand in the brush or someplace and then become motionless.
And then things begin to become alive.
And pretty soon you begin to see the squirrels and sparrows and raccoons and rabbits that were there all the time but just, you know, duck out of the way when you look at them too closely.
Meditation is like that.
You sit down and shut up and don't move.
And then the things in your mind begin to come out of their holes and start doing their running around and singing and so forth.
And you just let that happen.
I'd like to make contact with...*
It's as though in meditation we allow ourselves to become lost, to see things completely fresh, as if we encounter them for the first time without a frame or field of reference.
One of the things I like to do sometimes is get lost.

Go in the woods and spin around and then walk off in a direction and see how that feels, because it's a very interesting opening of all the normal frames of reference that we hold around ourselves all the time.
Step off the path into the open field or into the open woods.
I've often thought about how I have unnoticed frames of reference I may be situated within when I meditate.
We most often sit down within our limited view, which is unnoticed most of the time by us.
It's a circle within which we circle around, like having glasses on our face that we don't notice we're looking through.
Letting our attitudinal frame of reference slip away is sort of the heart of zazen, allowing wild perception to happen.
It's allowing awareness for a new species of feelings and thoughts, awareness of diversity.
I think Dogen might have been talking about this when he talked about dropping away of body and mind.
We say this very body is the Buddha and this very land is the Buddha land.
We are all, every being, intrinsically interconnected and enlightened.
Although there is no way to describe how that's so, or how anything came to be, or what happens beyond just this, there are still rules.
We all know that there are rules.
We have to treat each other and everything with care, in a just and fair way, with kindness, with some happiness, with love.
That's not every question.
If you've read some Thich Nhat Hanh, sometimes he'll say something like, sit down with a slight half smile.
It's as though, look, rather than just taking on an attitudinal frame of reference that you're not even aware of, let's take on one that you are aware of, a good one, a helpful one.
But how are we able to live in light of that idea as clearly as our insight, only as clear as our insight allows it to be?
So what's the nature of that insight?
How do we access it?
How do we deepen it?
It seems that the underlying attitude is radical openness, viewing over the whole of the landscape, open to seeing something we've never seen before, something for which we've yet to find a name.
So there's a bird that I've encountered and had some very interesting experiences with over the last couple of years.
It's a northern goshawk.
When we do the Christmas bird count for the Audubon Society, they always include a sheet that says, report any goshawk sightings.
They're rare, and they're trying to sort of pin down their nesting habits and whatnot.
It's a hawk almost the size of a red-tail, but it's not in the same order.
It's not a buteo with a fan tail and broad, soaring wings.
It's an accipiter with a narrow tail and shorter wings.
It's more agile.
It's a forest hawk.
It catches squirrels and birds on the wing.
And I'd never seen one.
But we were sitting at our camp up at Mount Baker with the Mountains and Rivers retreat a couple years ago.
We were eating dinner, sitting on some logs, surrounded by some very short alpine firs, only as tall as the ceiling here.
This hawk must have been swooping low over those trees looking for an opportunity to drop on something, and it came right up on us.
It didn't know we were there.
We didn't know it was there.
But all of a sudden, the fork is halfway to my mouth, and suddenly there's this bird there that's like this big.
The Rolodex in my mind is going, and I can't find a name.
I've never seen this bird before, and it's big.
And it's gone.
Tim had a [unclear: "birdie nap"] on his iPhone, and we were able to look it up pretty quick.
Technology.
Great.
Well, maybe a year later, I was doing work on my house.
I was up on a scaffolding, spending a couple of weeks up there, getting a really good view.
It's about this time of year, March.
I was witnessing almost every day some kind of aerial battle over the meadow between a pair of ravens and various types of raptors.
A bald eagle swooped in.
Two turkey vultures swooped in at one point.
Apparently these ravens were setting up the nesting territory on the far end there, which they have, and they've been raising young there for the last couple of years.
But there was a bird that swooped in a couple of times that I could barely catch a glimpse of.
I was just, whoa, it was fast, and it would just be in and out.
I didn't know what it was.
I thought it was a northern harrier because it looked like it had the white rump patch.
But really, I've never seen harriers at my field because it's not super open.
It's a lot of woods, so I just couldn't tell.
I had this inkling in my mind, I wonder if that's a northern goshawk.
Then a year later, my friend Jeff, who has a place a thousand feet through the woods off that way, calls me up one day and says, I've been seeing these hawks flying through the trees.
I have no idea what they are.
Come over and maybe we'll mess around, because I think they've got a nest over here.
So we went and messed around, and what we did is we ended up kicking up some red-tails who were screaming at us, and that was their nest.
I said, well, this isn't the ones, right?
He's describing them to me, and I'm going, that sounds like goshawks.
So we're sitting out on chairs on his front patio, just as it's really getting dusk and the light's sort of shining across the tops of the trees horizontally.
And he goes, there they are.
They flew right over us, right over the treetops, perfect with the light coming underneath them, so you just couldn't mistake it.
They were both heading into the forest block to roost for the night.
The mating pair of goshawks.
Several weeks later I had been away for a week, and I came home one day and slept in that morning.
I woke up in bed, and where I'm lying in bed, I've got a high window, higher on the wall like that.
From the bed I'm looking up, and there's a swamp, and there's a snag in the swamp, just sort of sticking up in the view of the window.
I'm just lying there in bed, and a goshawk just comes and lands on it.
So I run and get my binoculars, and I get back in bed, and now I'm looking at this goshawk from bed.
I'm thinking, well, this bird is starting to feel like more of a real thing.
I stepped out the door an hour later, and the two of them were playing chase tail each other and doing cartwheels over the pump house.
They were playing all through the meadow that whole day, and they've been gone ever since.
I don't know, they're around, you know, but suddenly this apparitional being had sort of forcefully presented itself and had become real.
It integrated itself into the world I inhabit and had become intimate.
Seeing out in the world, I don't really believe, is different than seeing in when we're on the cushion.
If that world is the Buddha land, then these encounters we have, these recognitions, are no different than the recognitions and encounters we have with the world that we inhabit in meditation.
It's the attitude of looking beyond far trees, beyond the differences in the shadows and the form, picking out the differences.
Perceiving the diversity of beings is really the heart of practice.
Do we really know anything, or is it all knowledge we just have, like filling up a bucket that sort of leaks out eventually, and what's left?
It's these encounters, it's these apparitions, these connections, the birth of the day.
So we have some field of work in our sitting where we can try to let those barriers that we might not know we carry with us go, and realize there's more.
There's always more that we don't know yet, that we haven't consciously encountered, that's beyond the thing we're working on, that we're cycling around.
Thanks.
